title: What killed Otto Vass?
article: Say this much about cadavers - they don't sue for malpractice.
That is the central issue now at a manslaughter trial in which four Toronto police officers have pleaded not guilty.

Dr. David Chiasson, the respected pathologist who conducted the exhaustive post-mortem, found the cause of death to be a fatty embolism - microscopic bits of fat that had dislodged and migrated into _Vass_' lungs, clogging blood vessels and leading to asphyxiation, this after the 55-year-old had received multiple blows during a short but violent episode with officers on Aug. 9, 2000.

The scuffle outside a west-end 7-Eleven had been thoroughly unexpected and, as court has heard from the only defendant thus far to take the stand, unprovoked - seemingly arising out of nothing beyond a brief conversation, with police asking to see _Vass_' identification following a low-priority called-in complaint about an "unwanted guest" on the premises. At first blush, the original two officers who'd responded to the call assumed _Vass_ had in fact been more victim than aggressor, judging by the welts on his face.

But _Vass_, as others have already testified, was a profoundly disturbed individual - his long-standing mental illness well- documented - with a predisposition towards violence, often hurting people who meant him no ill, including strangers and kindly interveners. On this particular evening, _Vass_ had already punched one young man in the head, a fellow idling in a car outside the convenience store. That shocking episode had prompted a retaliatory smack when the man, in the company of two friends, pursued _Vass_ into the store, one of them delivering a "glancing blow" upside _Vass_' head, before the three of them skedaddled, wanting no more of this bizarre encounter. Earlier that same evening, _Vass_ had jumped out of the van he was driving - causing it to hit a wall - complaining that there was a bomb inside the vehicle and that he could smell napalm.

Mental illness and its treatment is an imprecise science. One hopes for more from those who probe and analyze gross anatomy, which is what Chiasson did in the autopsy that followed, even if that's not always possible. And that's what Chiasson was aiming for. The then provincial deputy chief coroner-pathology, Chiasson was trying to determine why _Vass_ died, and died so quickly, while officers struggled to control him and apply handcuffs.
The scuffle had lasted only minutes yet _Vass_ had stopped breathing and could not be resuscitated by paramedics who arrived promptly at the scene.

It was no easy diagnosis for Chiasson. Indeed, his initial finding was that there was no definitive finding; that cause of death was "multifactorial," a combination of various elements but attributable to no one specific thing. It was only later, after consulting with a colleague, that Chiasson ran further "fat-stain" tests. These revealed striking, black stains on the lungs, a sign that fat had moved into the area, causing respiratory failure. The finding was something of a surprise because, Chiasson told the court, fatty embolisms are more common when a person has suffered broken bones. _Vass_ had blunt trauma injuries, lots of bruising and abrasions, but no broken bones. Chiasson ultimately concluded that fat from some of the soft-tissue injuries had entered the bloodstream and become trapped in the lungs. "We found lots of fat in the lung," he said from the witness box last week. Traces of fat were also found in the heart and in the meningeal vessels of the brain.

Yesterday, however, the defence called to the stand their own expert witness, a coroner with 50 years experience, thousands of autopsies under his belt, and author of many scholarly papers on fatty embolisms.

"My opinion is that there is indeed fat in some blood vessels, but that is not the cause of death," said Dr. Werner Spitz, a professor of pathology and for several decades a chief medical officer in Michigan.

Upon reviewing the coroner's report and Chiasson's testimony - though conducting no direct tests himself - Spitz said while there was some fat in the lung, it was "not an overwhelming amount" and could not have accounted for such a rapid death. Further, in the normal course of injuries where fatty embolisms cause death, it would take at least a day for the embolism to travel beyond the lung and lodge in the heart or meningeal vessels covering the brain.

Although there were fatty embolisms in the lung, _Vass_, while quite obese, should have been able to be resuscitated, he said. And the fact fatty matter had already travelled to _Vass_' heart and brain suggested it had been propelled there, probably by paramedics pounding on his chest It was not, in other words, the result of a shortscuffle with police. "I do not believe that the 31/2-minute (altercation) contributed significantly to the death."
Spitz posited a different theory. "The fact he died so rapidly, so suddenly, so inexplicably, I would characterize it as an electric death."

This he described as the heart generating too much power - whether from stress, over-excitement or over-exertion, maybe even due in part to _Vass_' underlying psychiatric illness - which it can't sustain for long.

"One minute he's fighting like crazy and the next minute he's stopped breathing. The heart responds to a surge of power, like a short circuit. At some point, the heart will give up, it will be exhausted, especially one that weighs 480 grams."
